main:
Breeze of Breslov

Parshat Lech Lecha | October 15-16, 2021

“Sarah’s Beauty”

Growing up, there were many obstacles I had to believing in the existence of G-d. Chief amongst them is why “bad things happen to good people”. This is a famous question and not one unique to me. It is a kasha that has been investigated for thousands of years by philosophers and theologians alike. In fact, Môshè Rabbeinu asked this very question to G-d Himself (Brachot 7a).

One of the problems with the question however, is the inherent and preconceived notion of what good is. When one begins to pour through Rebbe Nachman’s Torah, the assumed notion of good becomes flipped on its head and transformed. For the Rebbe, “good” is not what appears good or even what feels good. “Good” is nothing other than closeness to HaShem (Tehillim 73).

Once one internalizes real “good”, a paradigm shift begins to take place. What appeared to initially be “bad”; the events in our lives involving pain, cruelty, and trauma, chas v’shalom, ultimately becomes the very birth place of true good. For in truth, all distancing is only for the sake of being brought close (Likutey Moharan Tinyana 48)!

In Parshat Lech Lecha, this powerful dynamic comes to light. Our Sages teach us that Avraham’s life is a microcosm of every Jew’s life. And it is well documented that Avraham’s life was one of tremendous tests and challenges. I would like to examine one specific hardship which drives home the idea that apparent “bad” is merely concealed “good”.

HaShem had just communicated explicitly with Avraham for the first time, encouraging him to leave behind the comforts of his birthplace and trek to an unknown Land that only HaShem   could show him. However, as soon as Avraham arrives in Eretz Yisrael, a famine strikes and he is told to descend to Mitzrayim. This bizarre succession of events leads to the most unusual occurrence of all. 

As Avraham was taking his family down to Mitzrayim, the Torah points out that Avraham hadn’t truly appreciated how beautiful Sarah was. But they had been married for decades! The problematic nature of Avraham’s lack of perception is strengthened based on our Sages teaching that Sarah was one of the most beautiful women in history (Megillah 15A). Many answers are given by the commentators of the Torah to try and reconcile this difficulty, but none of them really leave you feeling satisfied.

Until a teaching of Rebbe Nachman dawned on me earlier this week. Rabbeinu teaches that Sarah uniquely embodies the quality of “Tefillah”, prayer, while Avraham embodies the “Tzaddik”, the lofty spiritual master (Likutey Moharan 10). Avraham and Sarah were inherently married, just as a Tzaddik is only a spiritual master due to his personal level of Tefillah. 

If we plug this secret in, we can begin to understand how Avraham, the Tzaddik, had never truly appreciated the tantalizing beauty of Sarah, Tefillah. The Gemara teaches that while prayer stands on the highest summit of existence, it is one of the things most overlooked by man (Brachot 6B). 

When does one begin to appreciate the incomparable beauty of prayer? 

Only when they go down to “Mitzrayim”, the place of suffering and servitude. 

I can vividly recall the most painful period of my life, sitting in a hospital bed after having checked myself into the local psych ward following three brutal years of major depression and debilitating psychosomatic symptoms. Through this period, it was only Rebbe Nachman’s Torah lessons and an indomitable willpower that had kept me alive. But to transition from barely surviving to truly living, I would need to come to the same realization as my forefather Avraham. That after all, Sarah really was beautiful. 

In my hospital gown with eyes stained from tears, I realized that the Torah, even the wisdom of Rebbe Nachman, could only allow me to survive. To live and thrive, I would need to actually take the Rebbe’s advice. I made a promise to HaShem from that day moving forward, I would actualize Rebbe Nachman’s greatest advice to us.

Sixty minutes of personal conversation a day with my Creator, speaking to HaShem as if He were my best friend. This was a practice I had previously held in contempt, but now it was my only hope left. I began to pour my heart to HaShem, throwing EVERYTHING on him, as if I had no where else to turn and no one else upon whom to rely (Sichot HaRan 2). 

Every sixty minutes of “Hitbodedut”, personal conversation with HaShem, took me out of another psycho-spiritual gate of despair. I began to recognize the transcendent beauty of Sarah. But it was only after having being sent down to my own personal “Mitzrayim”, that I could truly appreciate her. 

Avraham didn’t leave Mitzrayim empty-handed,  and neither had I. Avraham left laden with livestock. I left laden with real faith. All paradoxically accomplished through Sarah, heartfelt prayer. 

In a year in which we anxiously wait for our collective and personal Geulah, I bless each of us that we should work diligently and on a daily basis to cultivate Emunah through the daily practice of speaking to HaShem like He is your best friend. Because at the end of the day, Rabbeinu teaches that Redemption can only come about through Emunah, and Emunah can only be attained through Tefillah (Likutey Moharan 7). 

And lest you feel that this is a practice exclusive to Tzaddikim and therefore beyond your personal spiritual level, remember that the Torah refers to the Jewish people as “Kulam Tzaddikim”, all Tzaddikim. 

Every single Jew is a Tzaddik in potential. When you make an effort to recognize Sarah’s Beauty in your life, you will discover the Tzaddik inside of you and enter the Land that HaShem so desperately yearns to show you, the Land of Emunah!
